1.Why an 8-billion parameter model overflows an 80 GB GPU#

In bfloat16 inference, an 8.03B8.03\text{B}8.03B parameter model (Llama-3-8B) occupies 8.03×109×2 Bytes≈14.96 GB8.03 \times 10^9 \times 2\text{ Bytes} \approx 14.96\text{ GB}8.03×109×2 Bytes≈14.96 GB of VRAM. In mixed-precision training with AdamW, that same model requires 119.66 GB119.66\text{ GB}119.66 GB of static parameter-state memory before a single token's activations are even allocated.

The culprit is the 16Ψ16\Psi16Ψ Mixed-Precision Training Ledger (Rajbhandari et al., ZeRO, arXiv:1910.02054[2][2] · ZeRO · 2019ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter ModelsOpen arXiv:1910.02054 ↗). For every trainable parameter ψ∈{1,…,Ψ}\psi \in \{1, \dots, \Psi\}ψ∈{1,…,Ψ}:

  1. Working Weights (bfloat16 / float16): 2 Bytes2\text{ Bytes}2 Bytes per parameter used in forward and backward GEMMs.
  2. Gradients (bfloat16 / float16): 2 Bytes2\text{ Bytes}2 Bytes per parameter accumulated during backpropagation.
  3. Optimizer States (float32 AdamW):
    • Master copy of weights θfp32\theta_{\text{fp32}}θfp32​ (4 Bytes4\text{ Bytes}4 Bytes), required because small update steps Δθ=−ηm^t/v^t\Delta \theta = -\eta \hat{m}_t / \sqrt{\hat{v}_t}Δθ=−ηm^t​/v^t​​ underflow in 16-bit precision.
    • First moment momentum buffer mtm_tmt​ (4 Bytes4\text{ Bytes}4 Bytes).
    • Second moment variance buffer vtv_tvt​ (4 Bytes4\text{ Bytes}4 Bytes).
Static Training Memory=2Ψ⏟BF16 Weights+2Ψ⏟BF16 Grads+(4+4+4)Ψ⏟FP32 AdamW States=16Ψ Bytes\text{Static Training Memory} = \underbrace{2\Psi}_{\text{BF16 Weights}} + \underbrace{2\Psi}_{\text{BF16 Grads}} + \underbrace{(4 + 4 + 4)\Psi}_{\text{FP32 AdamW States}} = \mathbf{16\Psi\text{ Bytes}}Static Training Memory=BF16 Weights2Ψ​​+BF16 Grads2Ψ​​+FP32 AdamW States(4+4+4)Ψ​​=16Ψ Bytes
(1)

For a 70B70\text{B}70B model (Ψ=70×109\Psi = 70 \times 10^9Ψ=70×109), the static state alone requires 16×70 GB=1,120 GB16 \times 70\text{ GB} = \mathbf{1,120\text{ GB}}16×70 GB=1,120 GB—fourteen 80 GB80\text{ GB}80 GB H100 GPUs just to hold the static buffers, before accounting for layer activations!

2.ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3: Sharding redundant data-parallel state#

Standard Distributed Data Parallelism (DDP) replicates the entire 16Ψ16\Psi16Ψ byte state across all NdN_dNd​ data-parallel GPUs. Since every rank holds identical weights and optimizer buffers, Nd−1N_d - 1Nd​−1 copies are pure memory redundancy. Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) (arXiv:1910.02054[2][2] · ZeRO · 2019ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter ModelsOpen arXiv:1910.02054 ↗) partitions these three state components across the NdN_dNd​ data-parallel ranks while preserving the exact mathematical semantics of synchronous mini-batch SGD:

Sharding Mode Per-GPU Static Memory Formula 70B Model on Nd=8N_d = 8Nd​=8 GPUs Collective Communication Pattern & Overhead
Baseline DDP 16Ψ16\Psi16Ψ 1,120.0 GB1,120.0\text{ GB}1,120.0 GB (OOM) AllReduce gradients (2×2Ψ=4Ψ2 \times 2\Psi = 4\Psi2×2Ψ=4Ψ bytes per step)
ZeRO-1 (PosP_{\text{os}}Pos​) 2Ψ+2Ψ+12ΨNd2\Psi + 2\Psi + \frac{12\Psi}{N_d}2Ψ+2Ψ+Nd​12Ψ​ 385.0 GB385.0\text{ GB}385.0 GB ReduceScatter grads + AllGather updated weights (4Ψ4\Psi4Ψ bytes—zero extra traffic!)
ZeRO-2 (Pos+gP_{\text{os+g}}Pos+g​) 2Ψ+2Ψ+12ΨNd2\Psi + \frac{2\Psi + 12\Psi}{N_d}2Ψ+Nd​2Ψ+12Ψ​ 315.0 GB315.0\text{ GB}315.0 GB Gradients freed immediately after ReduceScatter (4Ψ4\Psi4Ψ bytes—zero extra traffic!)
ZeRO-3 / FSDP (Pos+g+pP_{\text{os+g+p}}Pos+g+p​) 16ΨNd\frac{16\Psi}{N_d}Nd​16Ψ​ 140.0 GB\mathbf{140.0\text{ GB}}140.0 GB (8×8\times8× reduction) Adds AllGather weights before forward & backward (1.5×1.5\times1.5× total traffic: 6Ψ6\Psi6Ψ bytes)

A ring or tree AllReduce of 2Ψ2\Psi2Ψ bytes of bfloat16 gradients is implemented under the hood as two phases:

  1. A ReduceScatter (2Ψ2\Psi2Ψ bytes transferred), after which each of the NdN_dNd​ GPUs holds the fully summed gradient for its assigned 1/Nd1/N_d1/Nd​ shard of parameters.
  2. An AllGather (2Ψ2\Psi2Ψ bytes transferred), which broadcasts the summed gradients to every GPU.

In ZeRO-2, each rank only updates the 1/Nd1/N_d1/Nd​ slice of AdamW states it owns. Therefore, after ReduceScatter finishes, each rank immediately steps its local FP32 AdamW shard and discards the rest of the gradients, then executes the AllGather on the newly updated bfloat16 weights instead of the gradients. Total network volume remains 2Ψ+2Ψ=4Ψ2\Psi + 2\Psi = 4\Psi2Ψ+2Ψ=4Ψ bytes per step—identical to DDP!

3.Megatron-LM: Tensor Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism#

When a single layer's weight matrix or activation footprint is too large, or when ZeRO-3's inter-node AllGather latency exceeds interconnect bandwidth, Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., arXiv:1909.08053[1][1] · Megatron-LM · 2019Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model ParallelismOpen arXiv:1909.08053 ↗) slices the transformer operators themselves across fast intra-node NVLink (900 GB/s900\text{ GB/s}900 GB/s on H100) using Tensor Parallelism (TP).

The key design goal of Megatron-LM is to partition a two-layer MLP or multi-head attention block without requiring communication in the middle of the nonlinear activation function:

  1. Column-Parallel Linear First Layer (W1W_1W1​): Split the weight matrix A∈RH×dffA \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_{\text{ff}}}A∈RH×dff​ column-wise across NtpN_{\text{tp}}Ntp​ GPUs as A=[A1,A2,…,ANtp]A = [A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{N_{\text{tp}}}]A=[A1​,A2​,…,ANtp​​]. Because GeLU⁡\operatorname{GeLU}GeLU or SiLU⁡\operatorname{SiLU}SiLU is an element-wise nonlinearity, it applies independently to each column shard:
[Y1, Y2]=[GeLU⁡(XA1), GeLU⁡(XA2)]\big[Y_1,\, Y_2\big] = \Big[\operatorname{GeLU}(X A_1),\, \operatorname{GeLU}(X A_2)\Big][Y1​,Y2​]=[GeLU(XA1​),GeLU(XA2​)]
(2)
  1. Row-Parallel Linear Second Layer (W2W_2W2​): Split the down-projection matrix B∈Rdff×HB \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times H}B∈Rdff​×H row-wise as B=[B1B2]B = \begin{bmatrix} B_1 \\ B_2 \end{bmatrix}B=[B1​B2​​]. The block matrix product becomes a sum of partial matrices:
Z=[Y1, Y2][B1B2]=Y1B1+Y2B2Z = \big[Y_1,\, Y_2\big] \begin{bmatrix} B_1 \\ B_2 \end{bmatrix} = Y_1 B_1 + Y_2 B_2Z=[Y1​,Y2​][B1​B2​​]=Y1​B1​+Y2​B2​
(3)

Each GPU computes YiBi∈RB×S×HY_i B_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times S \times H}Yi​Bi​∈RB×S×H locally, followed by a single AllReduce before the residual dropout and layer normalization. For Multi-Head Attention, WQ,WK,WVW_Q, W_K, W_VWQ​,WK​,WV​ are partitioned column-wise across heads, and WOW_OWO​ is partitioned row-wise—requiring only two AllReduce operations per Transformer block in the forward pass and two in the backward pass.

When scaling across multiple nodes connected by slower InfiniBand fabric, Pipeline Parallelism (PP) assigns contiguous groups of layers (stages) to different nodes. Naive sequential pipelining leaves Npp−1N_{\text{pp}} - 1Npp​−1 stages idle at any moment, creating a Pipeline Bubble fraction of Npp−1M+Npp−1\frac{N_{\text{pp}} - 1}{M + N_{\text{pp}} - 1}M+Npp​−1Npp​−1​ for MMM micro-batches. The 1F1B (One-Forward-One-Backward) schedule interleaves forward and backward micro-batches so that in-flight activation memory stays bounded by NppN_{\text{pp}}Npp​ micro-batches rather than MMM, while Sequence Parallelism (SP) shards the RMSNorm and Dropout activations along the sequence dimension SSS by replacing TP's AllReduce with ReduceScatter + AllGather.

4.Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Scaling vs. Inference-Optimal Models#

How should a fixed training compute budget C≈6NDC \approx 6 N DC≈6ND (where NNN is parameters and DDD is training tokens) be divided between model size NNN and dataset size DDD?

Kaplan et al. (2020) originally suggested scaling N∝C0.73N \propto C^{0.73}N∝C0.73 and D∝C0.27D \propto C^{0.27}D∝C0.27, leading to massive, under-trained models such as GPT-3 (175B175\text{B}175B parameters trained on 300B300\text{B}300B tokens) and Gopher (280B280\text{B}280B). Hoffmann et al. (Chinchilla, arXiv:2203.15556[3][3] · Chinchilla · 2022Training Compute-Optimal Large Language ModelsOpen arXiv:2203.15556 ↗) discovered that Kaplan's experiments used a fixed cosine learning-rate schedule length instead of matching the decay horizon to each token budget. By fitting the parametric loss surface across over 400 training runs:

Trained on 1.4T1.4\text{T}1.4T tokens, the 70B70\text{B}70B Chinchilla model outperformed the 280B280\text{B}280B Gopher model across virtually every benchmark while requiring 4×4\times4× less inference memory and compute.

4.1Why Llama-3 trains an 8B model on 15 Trillion tokens#

Notice that Chinchilla optimizes strictly for pretraining FLOPs CtrainC_{\text{train}}Ctrain​, ignoring lifetime inference cost CinferC_{\text{infer}}Cinfer​. Under the D≈20ND \approx 20ND≈20N rule, an 8B8\text{B}8B model is "compute-optimal" at just 160B160\text{B}160B tokens. Yet Meta trained Llama-3-8B on 15 Trillion15\text{ Trillion}15 Trillion tokens (D/N≈1,875×D / N \approx 1,875\timesD/N≈1,875×—nearly 94×94\times94× beyond the Chinchilla ratio!).

Why? Because a popular open-weights or production model is trained once, then served across billions of inference requests. Spending extra pretraining compute to compress the loss of a 70B70\text{B}70B Chinchilla-optimal model into an 8B8\text{B}8B parameter footprint permanently slashes every downstream user's KV cache footprint and decode HBM traffic by nearly 9×9\times9×. Modern frontier training therefore follows an Inference-Adjusted Scaling Law:

min⁡N,D  L(N,D)subject to6ND+2N⋅Tlifetime_infer≤Ctotal\min_{N, D}\; L(N, D) \quad \text{subject to} \quad 6 N D + 2 N \cdot T_{\text{lifetime\_infer}} \le C_{\text{total}}N,Dmin​L(N,D)subject to6ND+2N⋅Tlifetime_infer​≤Ctotal​
